Google tests a cuffless smartwatch check for high blood pressure A Google study suggests an ordinary smartwatch can flag likely high blood pressure without anyone strapping on a cuff first. The paper appeared in Nature, and in a trial with 196 adults the watch picked up more hypertension cases than a single reading at a doctor's office did. The numbers are modest, and Google says so. The watch caught 65.8% of the people who truly had hypertension, against 55.3% for the initial office screening, while specificity (correctly clearing healthy people) was 90%. When the watch said 'high', it was right 80.6% of the time, compared with 77.8% for office readings. The system uses two sensors nearly every smartwatch has: the optical pulse sensor and the accelerometer. Google Research says the accelerometer also picks up tiny vibrations of the wrist caused by each heartbeat. Google puts the number of hypertension sufferers worldwide above one billion and says most are unaware of it, especially people aged 18 to 44. The full results are in the Nature paper. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11336-3 https://techprolonged.com/2026/11/google-tests-a-cuffless-smartwatch-check-for-high-blood-pressure/

Google model spotted 65.8% of hypertension cases from smartwatch pulse and motion sensors in a 196-person study Google researchers have built a model that flags likely high blood pressure using only the optical pulse sensor and accelerometer in a consumer smartwatch, with no cuff for calibration. In a prospective study of 196 people at five US sites, published in Nature, it identified 65.8% of participants with hypertension at 90.0% specificity, while an initial office blood pressure measurement identified 55.3%. Both methods were scored against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which the researchers describe as the clinical gold standard. Participants had no known cardiovascular disease and were not taking blood pressure medication. The work was a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School. The model was pre-trained without diagnostic labels on 492,347 hours of photoplethysmography and accelerometer data from 2,109 participants. An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations Daily briefing, 2026-11-04, compiled Wed, 04 Nov 2026 18:44 UTC. The story: Researchers have developed an AI-native experimental laboratory called AutoDNA for autonomous biomolecular operations, according to a study published in Nature on November 4, 2026. The system was created by a team including researchers with ORCID identifiers and authors such as Jiabin Wang, Zhiyuan Dong, Jingkai Yang, Qingting Li and Tianyu Huang. AutoDNA is designed to carry out multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments with minimal human intervention. The work was published as an article in Nature with supporting data, code and supplementary information. The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to perform core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing. Human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks such as reagent and labware replenishment. Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields and accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.2-fold. It also completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation. The authors say AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing applications in synthetic biology and information storage. They describe the system as realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework through co-design of models, experiments and instruments. The paper frames the work as addressing a long-standing goal of AI-native laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention.

On November 4, 2026, a Shanghai Jiao Tong University team and collaborators published An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations in Nature, introducing AutoDNA. The architectural difference from earlier 'bolt-on' autonomous labs is decisive: AutoDNA uses multiple agents under a central Planner that coordinates specialists for literature search, reagent management, protocol design, code generation, hardware control, and hypothesis generation. Given a natural-language request, the system autonomously runs the full loop from literature search and reagent selection through experiment design, code generation, hardware execution, and result analysis. Two engineering pillars: a hardware abstraction layer and a digital twin. The system parses instrument manuals and abstracts device capabilities into natural-language 'atomic services' (a pipette, for example, becomes transfer and mix), after which a code agent generates control code and self-corrects. As a result, AutoDNA coordinates more than 20 instrument types and executes over 11,000 hardware operations at micron-level positioning and microliter-level liquid handling. Before execution, the system rehearses generated instrument code in a simulated environment, tracking liquid volumes and checking positions and settings; in one run, the simulation caught code attempting to read fluorescence before the sample container had been loaded, blocking the error ahead of costly real-world execution. Highlighted on the cover of Nature News by Heidi Ledford (DOI: 10.1038/d41586-026-03552-8) and analyzed in a Nature News and Views commentary by Stanford University Professor James Zou (DOI: 10.1038/d41586-026-03270-1), the platform executes complex nucleic acid synthesis, transcription, polymerase chain reaction amplification, and sequencing workflows from a single natural-language prompt. While artificial intelligence models can design candidate proteins and genetic sequences in minutes, validating those designs in a physical wet lab typically takes weeks or months of manual pipetting. Existing automated setups rely on rigid, task-specific scripts that struggle to coordinate diverse instruments. AutoDNA overcomes this bottleneck through a multi-agent operating system built on OpenHarmony that co-designs language-model reasoning, protocol generation, and real-time robotic scheduling. Across four benchmark demonstrations, AutoDNA optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis to a 97.8 percent yield, accelerated concurrent experimental protocols by 3.2-fold, completed a 203.5-hour end-to-end DNA digital data storage cycle across 78 DNA strands with 100 percent data recovery, and autonomously identified and validated a clinical KRAS G13D colorectal cancer mutation across 9,551 hardware steps.

Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting. Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting. The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics, which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering, is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Neel-order defects, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius-Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.
